title: Empty a food-processor bowl that still has its blade in
instruction: Put the chopped walnuts in the mixing bowl.
context: A food-processor S-blade only sits on its post: tip the bowl to pour and it slides out with the food, into the steadying hand or buried in the mixing bowl for the next hand. Taking it out first needs a straight 8 cm pull (more than 8 degrees off-axis, the sleeve wedges), then a 120-degree pour by the handle.
setup: Cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left). Clear 7-cup processor work bowl (KitchenAid KFP0718 type), 16 cm inside, 11.5 cm tall, 0.40 kg, base centred at (36, 9), loop handle toward the right arm; inside, 40 rigid walnut pieces of 9-13 mm (35 g) around the S-blade, whose black adapter (31 mm sleeve, 14 mm stem to 10.5 cm) sits loose on the 8.75 cm centre post (blade 0.10 kg, two steel arms reaching 7 cm). Blue melamine mixing bowl 22 cm inside, 9.5 cm tall, at (34, -19); green PE cutting board 30 x 20 cm at (40, 30); both fixed. Arms in the ready pose.
scoring: 0 if ever: the blade rides 2 cm up the post (or off it) with no gripper holding it, the blade is in the mixing bowl, falls off the table, or lies at rest unheld tilted over 45 degrees. Else score = walnut mass in the mixing bowl (not inside the work bowl) / 90%, capped at 1; x0.8 unless the blade ends seated on the post (within 1 cm) or released upright (within 20 degrees) on the board. 1.0 with the blade stowed, held 1 s, is success.
reset_notes: Seat the blade's adapter on the post, put the 40 walnut pieces back around it, set the bowl on its taped outline with the handle to the right. Handle the blade by its adapter with cut-resistant gloves.
fidelity: Approximate. Rigid boxes: 16-sided bowls, square post and stem, flat blade arms; mixing bowl and board fixed. 40 rigid walnut pieces (count kept low for fast, stable PhysX). The adapter slides on the post through a joint; its friction is computed each physics step from the sleeve's measured side load and tilt (beyond 1.5 deg play), set so a pull >8 deg off-axis wedges and a tipped bowl lets the blade go near 97 deg. Details in README.
